solution.concept_anchor: Statutory origin of Zonal Councils — States Reorganisation Act 1956
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students frequently conflate the constitutional recognition of cooperative federalism with the specific legal basis of Zonal Councils, assuming any major national body must be constitutional.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Zonal Councils appear nowhere in any constitutional article — they have no constitutional origin.
Confirm (b): Part V (Sections 15–22) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 explicitly establishes the Zonal Councils.
Eliminate (c): The Government of India Act, 1935, predates Indian independence and has no provision for Zonal Councils.
Eliminate (d): The Inter-State Council (Establishment) Order 1990 relates to the ISC under Article 263, not Zonal Councils.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students often assume that a body with such significant Centre-State coordination functions must derive authority from the Constitution itself. The trap here is the conflation of institutional importance with constitutional status. Finance Commission and Election Commission are genuinely constitutional bodies — Zonal Councils are not, despite performing a similar 'glue' function in Indian federalism. A partially prepared student who has read about Zonal Councils in the context of cooperative federalism may instinctively mark them as constitutional.
solution.final_explanation:
Zonal Councils are one of India's key Centre-State coordination mechanisms, yet their legal origin is statutory, not constitutional — a distinction that UPSC has repeatedly tested.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No article of the Constitution establishes Zonal Councils. Bodies like the Finance Commission (Article 280) and Election Commission (Article 324) are constitutional; Zonal Councils are not.
• Option (b) — Correct: Part V, Sections 15–22 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 established all five Zonal Councils. Being statutory means Parliament can modify or abolish them without a constitutional amendment.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Government of India Act, 1935, is a pre-independence colonial statute that established provincial autonomy and federal structures but has no provision for Zonal Councils.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Inter-State Council Establishment Order, 1990, operationalised the ISC under Article 263 — a completely separate body from Zonal Councils.

Value Addition:
• The Fazal Ali Commission (States Reorganisation Commission) recommended the zonal structure, which was then enacted via the 1956 Act.
• Being statutory also means Zonal Councils' composition and functions can be altered by ordinary legislation.
• The North-Eastern Council, a related body, was created under a separate statute — the North-Eastern Council Act, 1971.

solution.concept_anchor: Governors excluded from Zonal Council membership

statement_analysis.statement: The Union Home Minister serves as the Chairman of all five Zonal Councils simultaneously.
statement_analysis.reason: A single Union Home Minister chairs all five Zonal Councils — there is no separate chairman for each zone.

statement_analysis.statement: The Governor of each state in the zone is a permanent member of the respective Zonal Council.
statement_analysis.reason: Governors nominate members (Chief Minister + 2 ministers) to the Zonal Council but do not themselves sit as members — a critical distinction.

statement_analysis.statement: Chief Ministers of states rotate annually as Vice-Chairman of their respective Zonal Council.
statement_analysis.reason: The Vice-Chairmanship rotates among the Chief Ministers of states in that zone on an annual basis.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know the Governor has a formal role in nominating members may incorrectly extend that role to actual council membership.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — one Home Minister chairs all five councils, not zone-specific ministers.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Governors nominate members to the Council but are not members themselves; reject options that include Statement 2 as correct.
Statement 3 is correct — annual rotation of Vice-Chairmanship among CMs is an established structural feature.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct, pointing to option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the carefully engineered trap. Governors do have a formal role in Zonal Councils — they nominate the Chief Minister and two other ministers to represent each state. A student who has partially read about the membership structure will recall 'Governor' appearing and incorrectly conclude that Governors are members. The key precision is that nomination authority and membership are entirely different — a distinction this question directly exploits.
solution.final_explanation:
The membership architecture of Zonal Councils is a frequently tested structural detail, particularly the role of Governors.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Union Home Minister is the common Chairman of all five Zonal Councils. This centralised chairmanship underscores the Home Ministry's coordinating role in law, order, and inter-state affairs.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Governors are NOT members of Zonal Councils. Their role is to nominate the Chief Minister and two other ministers from each state to represent that state. Attending and nominating are entirely different functions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Vice-Chairmanship is not fixed — it rotates annually among the Chief Ministers of the states within that zone, ensuring equitable representation.

Value Addition:
• For Union Territories, the Administrator (Lt. Governor or Administrator) represents the UT on the Zonal Council.
• The distinction between 'nominating authority' (Governor) and 'member' is a classic UPSC precision trap.
• Each state sends its Chief Minister plus two ministers; the total membership of each council varies with the number of constituent states.

solution.concept_anchor: Central Zone — only zone with no Union Territory

statement_analysis.statement: Uttarakhand is a constituent state of the Western Zonal Council.
statement_analysis.reason: Uttarakhand is part of the Central Zonal Council, not the Western Zone, which comprises Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, and the UT of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu.

statement_analysis.statement: The Central Zonal Council is the only zone among the five that has no Union Territory in its composition.
statement_analysis.reason: The Central Zone (UP, Uttarakhand, MP, Chhattisgarh) has no associated Union Territory — making it unique among the five Zonal Councils.

statement_analysis.statement: Puducherry is represented in the Southern Zonal Council.
statement_analysis.reason: Puducherry, a Union Territory, is part of the Southern Zonal Council alongside Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students may be unsure about Puducherry's zonal placement and might incorrectly flag Statement 3 as wrong while missing that Statement 1 has the clear geographic error.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Uttarakhand borders UP and MP — it belongs to the Central Zone, not the Western Zone. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Check Statement 2: Central Zone (UP, Uttarakhand, MP, Chhattisgarh) has no UT attached — this is a well-known structural fact. Statement 2 is correct.
Check Statement 3: Puducherry is a UT adjoining Tamil Nadu and is part of the Southern Zonal Council. Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct — option (b) is the answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Uttarakhand's zonal placement is the geographic trap. Students may confuse Uttarakhand with states in the Western or Northern zone based on approximate geography. The states of the Western Zone (Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra) are on the western coast — Uttarakhand, a landlocked Himalayan state, belongs firmly in the Central Zone. Additionally, the 'no UT' characteristic of the Central Zone is an important factual distinction that rewards precise preparation.
solution.final_explanation:
Knowing which state belongs to which Zonal Council requires zone-by-zone memorisation — a favourite UPSC testing ground for geographic precision.

• Statement 1 — NOT Correct: Uttarakhand is part of the Central Zonal Council (along with UP, MP, and Chhattisgarh), not the Western Zone. The Western Zone comprises Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, and the UT of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Central Zonal Council is unique as the only zone among the five with no Union Territory — a structural fact worth memorising.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Puducherry, as a UT enclave within southern India, is appropriately placed in the Southern Zonal Council alongside the five southern states.

Value Addition:
• Northern Zone includes the UTs of Delhi, Chandigarh, and Ladakh — the highest UT count among zones.
• Eastern Zone (Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal) has no UT either — a secondary trap; only the Central Zone is commonly flagged for having none.
• J&K, now a UT, remains in the Northern Zonal Council after its reorganisation in 2019.

solution.concept_anchor: NEC — 8 states, separate from Eastern Zonal Council

statement_analysis.statement: The North-Eastern Council was established under the North-Eastern Council Act, 1971.
statement_analysis.reason: The NEC was created by the North-Eastern Council Act, 1971 — separate from the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 that created the five Zonal Councils.

statement_analysis.statement: Sikkim became a member of the North-Eastern Council upon its accession to India in 1975.
statement_analysis.reason: Sikkim was added to the NEC in 2002 — not in 1975 when it became a state — making this a temporal-swap trap.

statement_analysis.statement: The North-Eastern states are NOT part of any of the five original Zonal Councils — they are exclusively covered by the NEC.
statement_analysis.reason: The eight NE states (including Sikkim) are outside the five Zonal Councils' composition and are covered by the NEC, which has a broader regional planning mandate.

statement_analysis.statement: The NEC has a purely advisory mandate identical to that of the five Zonal Councils.
statement_analysis.reason: The NEC has a broader mandate including regional planning and development, unlike the Zonal Councils which are purely advisory in character.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 may be uncertain about Statement 4, tempting them to count three as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — NEC was established under the NEC Act, 1971, a separate statute from the 1956 Act.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Sikkim joined NEC in 2002, not in 1975 when it became India's 22nd state.
Statement 3 is correct — NE states have their own regional council (NEC) and are absent from the five Zonal Councils.
Statement 4 is incorrect — NEC has regional planning powers, going beyond mere advisory functions of the five Zonal Councils. Only two statements are correct — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two traps operate simultaneously. The Sikkim trap (Statement 2) conflates the year of Sikkim's accession to India (1975) with its inclusion in NEC (2002) — a 27-year gap that tests temporal precision. Statement 4 traps students who conflate NEC's mandate with that of the five Zonal Councils — both are statutory bodies but NEC has an additional regional planning and development mandate that makes it functionally distinct.
solution.final_explanation:
The NEC is structurally related to but functionally distinct from the five Zonal Councils — a nuanced distinction UPSC regularly exploits.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The NEC was created by the North-Eastern Council Act, 1971, a statute entirely separate from the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Sikkim's membership in the NEC dates to 2002 — a legislative amendment — not to 1975 when Sikkim merged with India as the 22nd state.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The eight NE states (Arunachal, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura) fall exclusively under the NEC, not the Eastern Zonal Council.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: NEC's mandate is broader — it includes regional planning, development coordination, and economic planning for the northeast, unlike the purely advisory Zonal Councils.

Value Addition:
• Originally NEC covered 7 states; Sikkim's addition in 2002 brought the total to 8.
• The NEC's broader mandate reflects the unique developmental challenges and strategic sensitivity of the northeastern region.
• The Eastern Zonal Council covers Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, and West Bengal — no northeastern state appears in it.

solution.concept_anchor: PM chairs ISC; Home Minister chairs Zonal Councils
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because it reverses the chairpersons of the ISC and Zonal Councils — the most common confusion point in this topic.
elimination_logic: Anchor on List I-A (Inter-State Council): ISC is established under Article 263 with the Prime Minister as Chairman — match with List II-2.
Anchor on List I-B (Zonal Councils): Home Minister chairs all five Zonal Councils — match with List II-4.
List I-C (Finance Commission): A constitutional body under Article 280, constituted by the President — match with List II-1.
List I-D (NEC): Established by a separate statute — the North-Eastern Council Act, 1971 — match with List II-3. This gives A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The primary trap is the chairperson-swap between the Inter-State Council and Zonal Councils. Many students remember that the Prime Minister is associated with inter-state coordination and incorrectly assign PM's chairmanship to Zonal Councils as well. In reality, the PM chairs the ISC while the Home Minister chairs all five Zonal Councils. This distinction carries political significance: the Home Minister's role reflects the law-and-order dimension of these councils.
solution.final_explanation:
This match-the-column tests precise knowledge across four distinct institutional bodies in Indian federal architecture.

Correct pairings:
• A (Inter-State Council) — 2 (Prime Minister as Chairman): ISC under Article 263 is chaired by the PM, with all Chief Ministers and relevant Cabinet Ministers as members.
• B (Zonal Councils) — 4 (Union Home Minister as Chairman): All five Zonal Councils share a single chairman — the Home Minister — reflecting their law, order, and coordination focus.
• C (Finance Commission) — 1 (Constituted by the President): The Finance Commission is a constitutional body under Article 280, appointed by the President every five years to recommend Centre-State revenue distribution.
• D (North-Eastern Council) — 3 (North-Eastern Council Act, 1971): The NEC derives its authority from a separate Act of Parliament, distinct from the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

Trap pairing: Option (a) reverses B and A — PM with Zonal Councils and HM with ISC — exploiting the most common confusion in this topic.

Value Addition:
• ISC was actually constituted only in 1990 under Article 263, despite the article existing since 1950.
• Finance Commission chairperson is appointed by the President; the body itself is constituted every five years.
• NEC secretariat is located in Shillong, Meghalaya.

solution.concept_anchor: Advisory nature of Zonal Councils — non-binding but politically effective
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually true, tempting students to assume the causal link without verifying whether advisory status causes political irrelevance or the opposite.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes — Zonal Council recommendations are non-binding on both the Centre and states; they are purely advisory.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? Yes — political consensus built through deliberation in Zonal Councils does feed into actual policy and legislation, establishing their real-world utility.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? No — R does not explain why recommendations are non-binding; it rather explains why non-binding status does not make the councils ineffective. The two are logically related but R is not the cause of A's advisory nature.
Both A and R are correct, but R does NOT explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This assertion-reason is engineered around a common reasoning shortcut: students see both A and R as true and reflexively select option (a). However, R speaks to the political effectiveness of Zonal Councils despite their advisory nature — it does not explain why recommendations are non-binding in the first place. The non-binding character flows from their statutory design, not from their political consensus-building function. Distinguishing causal explanation from contextual relevance is the precise skill this question tests.
solution.final_explanation:
The advisory character of Zonal Councils and their political effectiveness are two related but causally independent facts.

Assertion (A): Factually correct. Zonal Council recommendations carry no legal compulsion — states and the Centre may accept, partially implement, or ignore them without any formal consequence.

Reason (R): Factually correct. Despite non-binding recommendations, the deliberative process within Zonal Councils builds informal political consensus. This consensus often shapes policy decisions, budget allocations, and legislative action — demonstrating that advisory status does not equal ineffectiveness.

Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The non-binding character of Zonal Councils is a deliberate statutory design choice rooted in their consultative mandate under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. R, on the other hand, contextualises why this design still produces real outcomes. These are complementary facts, not cause and effect.

Value Addition:
• Contrast with GST Council — its decisions have quasi-binding practical effect even though it is also technically advisory.
• Sarkaria Commission (1988) and Punchhi Commission (2010) both endorsed strengthening Zonal Councils while retaining their advisory character.
• The ISC under Article 263 is similarly advisory — no constitutional body in India's federal framework has compulsory inter-state jurisdiction except the Supreme Court.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronological sequence — States Reorganisation to ISC to Punchhi Commission
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students may confuse the date of the Sarkaria Commission's constitution (1983) with the year of its report (1988), and may misplace NEC relative to the ISC.
elimination_logic: Anchor event 1: States Reorganisation Act was passed in 1956 — this creates Zonal Councils. It must come first.
Anchor event 2: NEC was created by the North-Eastern Council Act in 1971 — after 1956 but before 1990.
Anchor event 3: ISC was formally constituted in 1990 via Presidential Order under Article 263 — after NEC.
Anchor event 4: Punchhi Commission submitted its report in 2010 — the latest of all four events. Correct sequence: 1 → 3 → 2 → 4, which is option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The key temporal trap is the placement of the Inter-State Council (1990) relative to the North-Eastern Council Act (1971). Students who know Article 263 has existed since 1950 may incorrectly place the ISC before the NEC, not realising that the ISC was actually constituted only in 1990 despite the constitutional provision existing for four decades. The Punchhi Commission (2010) report date is less commonly memorised and tests whether students can distinguish commission constitution year from report year.
solution.final_explanation:
This chronology tests whether students know the operational dates — not just the existence — of key federal coordination institutions.

Correct sequence: States Reorganisation Act (1956) → North-Eastern Council Act (1971) → ISC constituted (1990) → Punchhi Commission report (2010)

• 1956: The States Reorganisation Act created the five Zonal Councils while simultaneously reorganising states on linguistic lines — two linked events.
• 1971: The North-Eastern Council Act created a separate regional body for the NE states, acknowledging their unique developmental context.
• 1990: The Inter-State Council was formally constituted under Article 263 via a Presidential Order — 40 years after the constitutional provision was enacted. This gap is itself a UPSC-worthy fact.
• 2010: The Punchhi Commission (on Centre-State Relations) submitted its report recommending Zonal Councils be empowered as the primary dispute-resolution forum before courts.

Value Addition:
• The Sarkaria Commission was constituted in 1983 and submitted its report in 1988 — it recommended Zonal Councils meet at least twice a year.
• Article 263 itself has existed since the Constitution came into force in 1950 — the ISC's late constitution in 1990 is a significant institutional fact.
• Sikkim was added to the NEC in 2002, decades after the NEC's formation.

solution.concept_anchor: UT representation in Zonal Councils — Administrator not CM
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students may reason that since UTs are under central administration, the Home Ministry directly represents them — conflating administrative oversight with formal council representation.
elimination_logic: Identify the governing rule: UTs without legislatures are represented by their Administrators; UTs with a legislature (like Delhi, Puducherry) have their Chief Minister as representative.
The new UT of Gadsimpur has a legislature — its Chief Minister participates. The newly carved UT without a legislature would send its Lt. Governor/Administrator.
Eliminate (a): It is incorrect that all UT representation is handled directly by the Ministry of Home Affairs — this conflates administrative control with Zonal Council representation.

Eliminate (b): Home Ministry does not 'directly represent' UTs at Zonal Council meetings — the Administrator or CM does. Eliminate (d): The Lt. Governor of the larger state is not relevant — the UT's own Administrator represents it. Confirm (c) as the correct principle.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students often assume that because UTs are under central administration, the Home Ministry speaks for them at Zonal Council meetings. The actual rule is more nuanced: UTs without legislatures send their Administrators (Lt. Governors or Administrators), while UTs with legislatures send their Chief Ministers. The scenario tests whether students can apply this distinction rather than defaulting to a simplistic 'UTs = Centre's proxy' logic.
solution.final_explanation:
Representation of Union Territories in Zonal Councils follows a rule that mirrors their governance structure on the ground.

The governing principle: A UT's representation in the Zonal Council depends on whether it has an elected legislature. UTs without a legislature (e.g., Chandigarh, Ladakh, Lakshadweep) are represented by their Administrators (Lt. Governors/Administrators). UTs with a legislature (Delhi, Puducherry) are represented by their Chief Ministers — consistent with how they are governed.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Ministry of Home Affairs provides secretariat support to Zonal Councils but does not directly represent UTs as a council member.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Home Ministry's administrative oversight over UTs is a separate constitutional arrangement and does not translate into proxy representation at Zonal Council meetings.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Lt. Governor (Administrator) of the UT without a legislature represents it at the Zonal Council, while a UT with a legislature sends its Chief Minister.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Lt. Governor of an adjoining state is irrelevant — each UT's own designated official represents it.

Value Addition:
• After J&K's reorganisation in 2019, J&K (with a legislature) and Ladakh (without) are both in the Northern Zonal Council — represented by CM and Lt. Governor respectively.
• Chandigarh (UT capital shared by Punjab and Haryana) is represented by its Administrator in the Northern Zonal Council.
• Central Zone remains the only zone with no UT representation whatsoever.

solution.concept_anchor: ISC under Article 263 vs. statutory Zonal Councils

statement_analysis.statement: The Inter-State Council established under Article 263 covers all states nationally, while Zonal Councils are zone-specific and operate at a regional level.
statement_analysis.reason: ISC is a national-level body with all Chief Ministers as members; Zonal Councils are regional bodies covering only the states and UTs within each zone.

statement_analysis.statement: Both the Inter-State Council and the Zonal Councils are constitutional bodies, with the ISC enjoying a higher constitutional standing due to its direct creation under Article 263.
statement_analysis.reason: Zonal Councils are statutory bodies created under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 — not constitutional bodies. The ISC is constitutional (Article 263), but Zonal Councils are not.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is unambiguously correct, leading students to assume Statement 2 must also be correct given both deal with the same institutional landscape.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: ISC under Article 263 is indeed a national body with all CMs; Zonal Councils are zone-specific. Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: The claim that 'both are constitutional bodies' is factually wrong. Zonal Councils are statutory — created under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, the answer is option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a partial truth that makes it deceptive — it correctly notes the ISC's constitutional standing (true) but falsely extends constitutional status to Zonal Councils as well. A student who knows the ISC is constitutional but is fuzzy on Zonal Councils' statutory origin will accept Statement 2 entirely. The key is precision: one body is constitutional, the other is statutory, and conflating them is the target trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional versus statutory distinction between the ISC and Zonal Councils is a high-frequency UPSC testing area.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The ISC under Article 263 is a nationally constituted body whose members include all Chief Ministers, Cabinet Ministers handling inter-state matters, and the Prime Minister as Chairman. Zonal Councils are regional, zone-specific platforms with the Home Minister as chairman — a narrower geographical and institutional scope.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Zonal Councils derive their existence from Part V (Sections 15–22) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 — an ordinary parliamentary statute. They are not constitutional bodies. The ISC alone is constitutional (Article 263). This means Parliament can modify or dissolve Zonal Councils without amending the Constitution, whereas abolishing the ISC's constitutional basis would require a constitutional amendment.

Value Addition:
• ISC was constituted only in 1990 via a Presidential Order — 40 years after Article 263 came into force.
• Being a constitutional body does not automatically make a body's decisions binding — ISC is also advisory.
• Zonal Councils' statutory status means their composition, functions, and even their existence can be altered by ordinary legislation.

solution.concept_anchor: Standing Committees of Zonal Councils — Chief Secretaries
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students familiar with the Home Minister's chairmanship may assume the Home Secretary chairs preparatory committees, confusing administrative head with secretariat-level committee membership.
elimination_logic: Identify who does the preparatory groundwork: it is senior civil servants at the Chief Secretary level, not elected representatives.
Eliminate (b): Additional Secretaries from the Planning Commission is anachronistic (Planning Commission was dissolved in 2014) and incorrect.
Eliminate (c): Home Secretaries of the constituent states are not described as heading the Standing Committees — this is a plausible but fabricated formulation.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Home Secretary option is engineered to exploit students' knowledge that the Home Ministry runs the Zonal Council secretariat. Students may reason that if the Home Minister chairs the full council, the Home Secretary must chair the preparatory committee — a logical but incorrect inference. The actual composition of Standing Committees involves Chief Secretaries of the constituent states, reflecting that the real deliberative work is done at the senior civil servant level before political leadership meets.
solution.final_explanation:

Value Addition:
• Standing Committees are the operational engine of Zonal Councils — full Council meetings are infrequent and largely ceremonial.
• Ministry of Home Affairs provides secretariat support to all five Zonal Councils from New Delhi.
• The UPSC angle: questions on 'who does the real work' in Zonal Councils point to Standing Committees, not the full Council.

solution.concept_anchor: Sarkaria Commission — twice a year meetings recommendation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because it correctly attributes the recommendation to the Sarkaria Commission but assigns the wrong frequency, exploiting imprecise memory.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Sarkaria Commission recommended meetings 'at least twice a year', not 'at least four times a year' — frequency is incorrect.
Confirm (b): Sarkaria Commission (1988) + 'at least twice a year' is the factually accurate pairing.
Eliminate (c): The Punchhi Commission (2010) recommended Zonal Councils as primary dispute forums before courts — not a meeting frequency recommendation assigned here.
Eliminate (d): 'Once every three years' is a fabricated and implausibly low frequency — no commission recommended this.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is frequency precision — 'twice a year' versus 'four times a year' versus 'once a year'. Students who remember 'Sarkaria Commission recommended more frequent meetings' without retaining the specific frequency will be vulnerable to option (a), which sounds plausible but is wrong. The question requires exact recall, not approximate memory.
solution.final_explanation:
Commission recommendations on Zonal Councils are frequently tested in UPSC — precision on 'who recommended what' is essential.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Sarkaria Commission is correctly identified but the recommended frequency of 'at least four times a year' is fabricated. The actual recommendation was 'at least twice a year'.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State Relations (1988) recommended that Zonal Councils should meet at least twice a year to maintain their relevance as cooperative federalism forums.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Punchhi Commission (2010) recommended that Zonal Councils be empowered as the primary forum for inter-state disputes before parties approach courts — a different type of recommendation from a meeting-frequency prescription.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: No commission recommended meetings 'once every three years' — this would render Zonal Councils operationally meaningless.

Value Addition:
• Sarkaria Commission was constituted in 1983 and submitted its report in 1988 — a five-year exercise on Centre-State relations.
• Punchhi Commission was constituted in 2007 and submitted its report in 2010.
• Both commissions characterised Zonal Councils as 'underutilised instruments of cooperative federalism'.

Advisory Nature and Non-Binding Character of Zonal Council Recommendations

solution.concept_anchor: Zonal Councils — consultative functions, no legislative or adjudicative power

statement_analysis.statement: Zonal Councils are empowered to discuss matters relating to the maintenance of public order within the zone.
statement_analysis.reason: Maintenance of public order in the zone is explicitly within the mandate of Zonal Councils under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

statement_analysis.statement: Zonal Councils can recommend cooperative management of inter-state infrastructure such as river systems and transport networks.
statement_analysis.reason: Recommending cooperative management of shared inter-state infrastructure is a core function of Zonal Councils — they serve as a deliberative forum for such matters.

statement_analysis.statement: A Zonal Council can issue binding directives to a state government regarding the implementation of an inter-state transport agreement.
statement_analysis.reason: Zonal Councils are purely advisory/consultative bodies — they cannot issue binding directives to any state government or the Centre under any circumstance.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 2 as correct may assume Statement 3 must also be correct given the 'all three' option is available, succumbing to overconfidence.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — public order maintenance is within the stated mandate of Zonal Councils.
Statement 2 is correct — recommending inter-state infrastructure management is a core deliberative function.
Statement 3 is incorrect — 'binding directives' directly contradicts the advisory/consultative character of Zonal Councils. Reject any option including Statement 3 as correct.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses the qualifier 'binding directives' — a direct contradiction of the non-binding advisory character of Zonal Councils. Students who have partially memorised that Zonal Councils 'deal with inter-state transport agreements' may not catch that the word 'binding' transforms a true function into a false one. This is a classic scope-extension trap where a real function is mischaracterised by adding an attribute the body does not possess.
solution.final_explanation:
The mandate of Zonal Councils is broad in subject matter but strictly limited in legal force — a distinction UPSC regularly tests.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Public order maintenance is part of the Zonal Council's discussion agenda. This reflects the Home Minister's role as Chairman and the security dimension of these bodies.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Zonal Councils serve as forums to deliberate and recommend cooperative management of inter-state infrastructure — rivers, roads, electricity grids. These recommendations go to the Centre and states for implementation.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Zonal Councils cannot issue binding directives to anyone — state or Centre. All outputs are recommendations. If states ignore them, there is no enforcement mechanism. Adjudicatory and legislative powers are entirely outside their mandate.

Value Addition:
• Economic and social planning, linguistic minority protection, and border disputes are other agenda items for Zonal Councils.
• River water disputes, despite being inter-state, have a separate adjudicatory mechanism under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 — Zonal Councils supplement but do not replace this.
• The 'purely consultative' nature is what distinguishes Zonal Councils from courts, Parliament, and even the GST Council.

Frequency of Meetings and Operational Reality

solution.concept_anchor: No mandatory meeting frequency — criticism of infrequency

statement_analysis.statement: The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 mandates that each Zonal Council must meet at least twice annually, with attendance by the Home Minister being compulsory.
statement_analysis.reason: No mandatory meeting frequency is prescribed in the Act — meetings depend on political will. The 'twice a year' frequency was a recommendation by the Sarkaria Commission (1988), not a statutory mandate.

statement_analysis.statement: Zonal Councils have no enforcement mechanism — a state that ignores a Zonal Council recommendation faces no formal legal or constitutional consequence.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an accurate description of the limitation — the purely advisory nature means there is no penalty or enforcement mechanism for non-compliance.

statement_analysis.statement: Critics have argued that with the Union Home Minister as the permanent Chairman, Zonal Councils cannot function as genuinely federal forums since the Centre's representative always presides.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a recognised criticism — the Home Minister's permanent chairmanship is seen by some as evidence of central dominance, undermining the spirit of federal parity.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know the Sarkaria Commission recommended 'twice a year' meetings may incorrectly assume this recommendation was legislatively incorporated, making Statement 1 seem correct.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: The 'twice a year' recommendation is from the Sarkaria Commission (1988), not the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. No statutory mandatory frequency exists. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Check Statement 2: No enforcement mechanism for Zonal Council recommendations is a factually accurate limitation. Statement 2 is correct.
Check Statement 3: The criticism of central dominance through the Home Minister's permanent chairmanship is a documented critique. Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct — answer is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a precisely engineered plausible-fabrication: it takes a real recommendation (Sarkaria Commission's 'twice a year' advice) and falsely elevates it to a statutory mandate. Students who have read about Sarkaria's recommendation may accept the 'twice a year' frequency as correct without noticing that the question claims it is part of the Act itself. The additional detail about 'compulsory attendance by the Home Minister' adds to the plausibility while being entirely fabricated.
solution.final_explanation:
The gap between design intent and operational reality is one of the key critique dimensions of Zonal Councils.

• Statement 1 — NOT Correct: The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 prescribes no mandatory meeting frequency. The 'at least twice a year' frequency is a Sarkaria Commission recommendation (1988) that remains largely unimplemented — it was never enacted into law. Compulsory attendance by the Home Minister is also not mandated.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The absence of an enforcement mechanism is a genuine structural limitation. States may ignore Zonal Council recommendations entirely with no legal repercussion.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The permanent chairmanship by the Union Home Minister is a structurally significant feature. Critics argue this makes Zonal Councils more Centre-centric than genuinely federal — states cannot set the agenda or chair the proceedings.

Value Addition:
• Some Zonal Councils went several years without meetings historically — a key criticism of their operational utility.
• Post-2014, meetings have been regularised, with Zonal Councils used as forums for cooperative federalism initiatives like 'One Nation One Ration Card'.
• Overlapping mandates with ISC and Finance Commission contribute to institutional redundancy — another criticism.

solution.concept_anchor: NDC defunct post-NITI Aayog 2015; Zonal Councils' renewed importance

statement_analysis.statement: The National Development Council (NDC) was effectively made defunct with the establishment of NITI Aayog in 2015.
statement_analysis.reason: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in January 2015; the NDC, which was linked to the Planning Commission's planning functions, has not met since and is considered effectively defunct.

statement_analysis.statement: Both the NDC and Zonal Councils had the Union Home Minister as the common presiding officer.
statement_analysis.reason: The NDC was chaired by the Prime Minister (not the Home Minister) and included all Chief Ministers — it was a national-level planning body, not a law-and-order coordination forum.

statement_analysis.statement: With the NDC's effective dissolution, Zonal Councils have gained renewed importance as regional Centre-State economic coordination forums.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-2015, Zonal Councils have increasingly been used for economic coordination topics previously covered by the NDC, reinforcing their relevance.

statement_analysis.statement: NITI Aayog's Governing Council partially fulfils the national coordination role previously held by the NDC, while Zonal Councils continue as the regional coordination mechanism.
statement_analysis.reason: NITI Aayog's Governing Council (chaired by PM, all CMs as members) mirrors the NDC's composition and partially fills its national coordination role; Zonal Councils remain the regional complement.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is the correct answer, which is also the strong distractor — students who are uncertain about Statement 2 may count all four as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — NDC's operational mandate lapsed with the Planning Commission's dissolution in 2015.
Statement 2 is incorrect — NDC was chaired by the Prime Minister, not the Home Minister. Reject any option counting Statement 2 as correct.
Statement 3 is correct — the relevance argument about Zonal Councils gaining importance is supported by post-2014 meeting regularisation.
Statement 4 is correct — NITI Aayog Governing Council as PM-chaired national coordination body fills the NDC's role. Three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the confusion between who chairs the Zonal Councils (Home Minister) and who chaired the NDC (Prime Minister). Students who associate all large coordination bodies with the Prime Minister may mark Statement 2 as correct. Alternatively, students who know the Home Minister chairs Zonal Councils may incorrectly assume the same arrangement applied to the NDC — a conflation trap between two different bodies.
solution.final_explanation:
The NDC-NITI Aayog-Zonal Councils triangle is an evolving institutional landscape that UPSC tests from multiple angles.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Planning Commission was dissolved in January 2015 and replaced by NITI Aayog. The NDC, which derived its significance from the national planning process, has not convened since and is effectively non-functional.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The NDC was chaired by the Prime Minister and included all Chief Ministers, Cabinet Ministers, and Planning Commission members. The Home Minister chairs Zonal Councils — these are two different bodies with different chairpersons.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Post-2014 regularisation of Zonal Council meetings, including discussions on GST implementation and internal security, reflects their expanded role filling part of the vacuum left by NDC.
• Statement 4 — Correct: NITI Aayog's Governing Council (PM as Chairman, all CMs as members) structurally mirrors the NDC and handles national-level coordination, complementing the regional role of Zonal Councils.

Value Addition:
• NDC last met in 2013 — over a decade without a formal meeting before being effectively replaced.
• NITI Aayog itself has no fiscal transfer authority — unlike the erstwhile Planning Commission.
• Zonal Councils' regional focus makes them irreplaceable for zone-specific issues even as NITI Aayog handles national coordination.

solution.concept_anchor: River water disputes — separate Tribunals, not Zonal Councils
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R sound correct and causally related to students who know that Zonal Councils discuss inter-state disputes and that river water disputes involve multiple states.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes — Zonal Councils provide an informal diplomatic channel for inter-state border disputes before formal judicial or presidential intervention.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? No — Inter-state river water disputes are adjudicated by Tribunals constituted under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 — a completely separate mechanism from Zonal Councils. R incorrectly identifies the primary adjudicatory mechanism.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer must be option (c) — A is correct but R is incorrect.
Correct option is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Reason sounds plausible because Zonal Councils do discuss river-related matters and inter-state infrastructure. However, the Reason specifically claims Zonal Councils are 'the primary mechanism for adjudicating river water sharing disputes' — which is factually wrong. The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 created separate Tribunals (like the Cauvery Tribunal, Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal) for this purpose. Conflating Zonal Councils' informal discussion role with formal adjudicatory authority is the trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between informal deliberation and formal adjudication is critical when applying Zonal Councils to specific dispute categories.

Assertion (A): Factually correct. Zonal Councils function as a soft diplomatic channel — a space where states can raise border disputes, discuss grievances, and seek consensus before the matter escalates to courts or parliamentary intervention. Examples include the Karnataka-Maharashtra border dispute (Belgaum) and Punjab-Haryana disputes discussed in respective Zonal Council settings.

Reason (R): Factually incorrect. Inter-state river water disputes are governed by the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, which provides for the constitution of dedicated Tribunals (e.g., Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal). Zonal Councils are not the primary mechanism and have no adjudicatory authority over river water sharing.

Since A is correct but R is factually wrong, option (c) applies.

Value Addition:
• The Supreme Court can also adjudicate inter-state river water disputes under Article 131 (original jurisdiction).
• Belgaum/Belagavi dispute involves Karnataka and Maharashtra — both in different Zonal Councils (South and West), illustrating a cross-zone limitation.
• River water Tribunals' awards are binding and published in the Gazette — unlike Zonal Council recommendations.

solution.concept_anchor: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 — both AP and Telangana in Southern Zone

statement_analysis.statement: Following the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, both the newly formed state of Telangana and the residual Andhra Pradesh are members of the Southern Zonal Council.
statement_analysis.reason: Both successor states — Telangana and residual AP — were placed in the Southern Zonal Council, which already included Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Puducherry.

statement_analysis.statement: The AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 required a constitutional amendment to create Telangana, since the bifurcation of an existing state into two states necessitates amendment of the First Schedule of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Creation of a new state by bifurcating an existing state requires amendment of the First Schedule (list of states) which is done under Article 3 read with Article 4 — technically a parliamentary statute that has the effect of amending the Constitution but does not require the special amendment procedure of Article 368.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because Statement 2 involves the nuanced Article 3/Article 4 procedure which students may incorrectly simplify as 'not requiring a constitutional amendment' and therefore mark Statement 2 as incorrect.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Both AP and Telangana fall within the geographic and administrative scope of the Southern Zonal Council — this is factually correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Article 3 allows Parliament to create new states; the consequential amendment of the First Schedule is covered by Article 4, which requires only a simple majority — it is still technically a constitutional amendment, though a simplified one. Statement 2 is correct in its essential claim.
Both statements are correct — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the Article 3/4 amendment procedure nuance. Students who know that creating a new state does NOT require the special majority under Article 368 may conclude that 'no constitutional amendment' is needed — and mark Statement 2 as incorrect. In fact, the First Schedule is amended, but through the simpler procedure under Article 4, which expressly provides that such amendments shall not be deemed to be amendments under Article 368. Both the claim and its nuance are testable UPSC material.
solution.final_explanation:
The Telangana bifurcation tests knowledge across both Zonal Council administration and the constitutional mechanics of state reorganisation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Southern Zonal Council now has six constituent states (AP, Telangana, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu) plus Puducherry — both successor entities from the 2014 bifurcation are in the same Zonal Council, which has made its meetings particularly contentious given unresolved water-sharing and asset-division disputes.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Creating Telangana required Parliament to pass the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014, under Article 3. Article 4 provides that such legislation amends the First and Fourth Schedules of the Constitution but does NOT require the special procedure of Article 368 — a simple majority suffices. So a constitutional amendment does occur, but through the simplified route.

Value Addition:
• Article 3 is the exclusive mechanism for Parliament to create new states, increase/decrease areas, change boundaries, or rename states.
• The consent of the state legislature concerned is not binding — Parliament may override objections after giving an opportunity to express views.
• Southern Zonal Council's post-2014 challenges (AP-Telangana water disputes) illustrate why Zonal Councils must adapt to new state creations.

States Reorganisation Act, 1956 — Legislative Basis and Part V

solution.concept_anchor: Zonal Councils — Nehru's 'one nation' integrative vision post-linguistic reorganisation
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because it correctly identifies states reorganisation on linguistic lines as the context but reverses the causal logic — Zonal Councils were the integrative response to linguistic reorganisation, not a precursor to it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Partition of 1947 preceded the States Reorganisation Act by nearly a decade and is not the immediate political context for Zonal Councils.
Confirm (b): Zonal Councils were deliberately created alongside the 1956 linguistic reorganisation as an integrative counterweight — Nehru's 'one nation' insurance against regional fragmentation.
Eliminate (c): Zonal Councils were not designed to replace the Constituent Assembly or fill a vacuum post-Constituent Assembly — this is a fabricated causal link.
Eliminate (d): Zonal Councils followed linguistic reorganisation as a corrective measure, not as a trigger for it — the sequence is reversed in this option.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) reverses cause and effect — it implies Zonal Councils were created so that linguistic states could then be created, whereas historically the opposite is true: states were reorganised on linguistic lines first (concerns about fragmentation arose), and Zonal Councils were the simultaneous integrative mechanism designed to hold the nation together within that new framework. Students who know both facts but not their causal relationship will select (d).
solution.final_explanation:
The political motivation behind Zonal Councils is as important as their institutional structure for UPSC.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: While Partition shaped India's early federal architecture broadly, the immediate context for Zonal Councils was the linguistic reorganisation of 1956 — a decade after Partition.
• Option (b) — Correct: Jawaharlal Nehru was concerned that reorganising states on linguistic lines could encourage regionalism and weaken national unity. Zonal Councils were the simultaneous corrective — a forum to foster 'one nation' spirit, discuss common inter-state concerns, and prevent new state identities from calcifying into separatism.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Constituent Assembly completed its work in 1949; Zonal Councils (1956) were not designed as a successor body to it.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: This reverses the sequence. Linguistic states came first; Zonal Councils were the integrative response, not the precondition for reorganisation.

Value Addition:
• The Fazal Ali Commission (States Reorganisation Commission) recommended the zonal structure alongside linguistic reorganisation.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because the National Governors Association is a real body in the USA, but it is a non-governmental organisation — not a government coordination mechanism equivalent to India's Zonal Councils.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): National Governors Association (USA) — it is non-governmental, not a formal federal coordination body equivalent to India's Zonal Councils.
Eliminate (b): Germany's Bundesrat is not a coordination body comparable to Zonal Councils — it is the upper house of Parliament representing states in the federal legislative process.

Eliminate (d): The European Council is an EU institution, not a federal coordination body within a single nation — it is not comparable to Zonal Councils.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) deploys an entity-swap trap — the National Governors Association is real and US-based, but it is a voluntary non-governmental body, not a formal intergovernmental coordination mechanism. The question requires knowing that the USA has no direct governmental equivalent to India's Zonal Councils.
solution.final_explanation:

• Option (d) — Incorrect: The European Council is an EU institution coordinating member states — it operates at a supra-national, not intra-national federal level.

• India's Zonal Councils are unique globally in having the interior/home minister (not PM) as chairperson — reflecting their security-coordination dimension.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 263 — ISC constitutional body; Zonal Councils — statutory under 1956 Act
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students aware that cooperative federalism has constitutional underpinnings may conflate Article 263's ISC with the Zonal Councils, assuming both are constitutional.
elimination_logic: Identify the structural distinction: ISC is the constitutional body under Article 263 with PM as Chairman; Zonal Councils are statutory under the 1956 Act with Home Minister as Chairman.
Eliminate (a): Article 263 establishes the Inter-State Council — not the Zonal Councils. Inserting 'Article 263' in the blank would be factually wrong.
Eliminate (c): Article 280 establishes the Finance Commission — unrelated to Zonal Councils.
Eliminate (d): No article of the Constitution establishes Zonal Councils — they are statutory. Confirm (b): 'States Reorganisation Act, 1956' is the correct answer filling the blank.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap here merges the ISC (Article 263, constitutional) with Zonal Councils (statutory). Students who broadly associate inter-state coordination with Article 263 will instinctively choose option (a). The question requires the student to correctly distinguish the ISC from Zonal Councils and recall that Zonal Councils have a statutory, not constitutional, origin.
solution.final_explanation:
The legal instrument establishing Zonal Councils is a foundational fact that distinguishes them from constitutional coordination bodies.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 263 of the Constitution establishes the Inter-State Council — a national-level body chaired by the Prime Minister. Filling the blank with 'Article 263' would make the sentence describe the ISC, not Zonal Councils.
• Option (b) — Correct: Zonal Councils were established under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 — specifically Part V, Sections 15–22. This statutory origin means Parliament can modify or abolish them through ordinary legislation.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 280 establishes the Finance Commission — a constitutional body appointed by the President to make recommendations on revenue distribution. Entirely unrelated to Zonal Councils.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: No provision of the Constitution creates Zonal Councils. Selecting 'Article 371' (special provisions for certain states) or any other article would be factually wrong.

Value Addition:
• Zonal Councils' statutory status contrasts with the Finance Commission (Art. 280), Election Commission (Art. 324), and ISC (Art. 263) — all constitutional.
• Being statutory, Zonal Councils' modification requires a simple parliamentary majority — no state ratification needed.
• The Fazal Ali Commission's report formed the intellectual basis for the 1956 Act's zonal provisions.

Role of Union Home Minister as Common Chairman

solution.concept_anchor: Home Minister chairs Zonal Councils; PM chairs ISC — not interchangeable
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who associate major Centre-State coordination with the Prime Minister may assume the PM co-chairs or presides when the Home Minister is unavailable.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable rule: Under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, the Union Home Minister is the designated Chairman of all five Zonal Councils — no deputy Chair from the PM's office is mentioned.
The Vice-Chairman is the rotating Chief Minister, not the Prime Minister or any central minister other than the Home Minister.
Eliminate (a): The PM does not co-chair or substitute as Chair of Zonal Councils — PM chairs the ISC, a different body.

Eliminate (b) and (d): No provisions for a senior Chief Minister or the state Chief Secretary to chair in the Home Minister's absence. Confirm (c): The rotating Vice-Chairman (Chief Minister of a constituent state) presides in the Home Minister's absence.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario creates a vacancy at the top and tests whether students know the substitution rule. The PM-substitute option is the trap: students conflate the PM's role in the ISC with Zonal Councils, assuming the PM is the natural fallback when the Home Minister is absent. The actual fallback under Zonal Council structure is the rotating Vice-Chairman — a Chief Minister of a constituent state — reinforcing the federal character even in the Home Minister's absence.
solution.final_explanation:
The chairmanship architecture of Zonal Councils has a built-in federal substitute that is structurally significant.

The applicable rule: The Union Home Minister is the permanent Chairman of all five Zonal Councils. The Vice-Chairmanship rotates annually among the Chief Ministers of the constituent states. When the Chairman is absent or unavailable to preside, the Vice-Chairman (the currently rotating Chief Minister) presides over the meeting.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Prime Minister chairs the Inter-State Council (Article 263), not Zonal Councils. There is no formal provision for the PM to step in as Zonal Council Chair when the Home Minister is absent.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The longest-serving Chief Minister has no formal seniority-based role in Zonal Council proceedings — the Vice-Chairmanship is determined by annual rotation, not tenure.
• Option (c) — Correct: The rotating Vice-Chairman (the Chief Minister who holds the Vice-Chair that year) presides when the Home Minister cannot attend — ensuring federal representation at the top even in the Chairman's absence.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Chief Secretary is a civil servant who supports the Standing Committee — they do not preside over the full Zonal Council meeting.

Value Addition:
• Annual rotation of Vice-Chairmanship ensures all states get a turn at leadership within the zone.
• The substitution rule reinforces that Zonal Councils are not entirely Centre-controlled — a state-level Chief Minister can chair proceedings.
• ISC has no equivalent rotation — the PM always presides; this is a structural difference worth noting.

solution.concept_anchor: Institutional redundancy criticism — GST Council is not a federal coordination body like Zonal Councils
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because the Finance Commission does overlap somewhat with Zonal Council discussions on fiscal federalism, but it is a constitutionally mandated body with a distinct function.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: bodies whose overlapping mandate with Zonal Councils has been cited as a criticism of institutional redundancy.
ISC (option a) — overlapping mandate: Yes, both discuss inter-state coordination at the national/regional level. Overlapping mandate criticism applies.

GST Council (option b) — overlapping mandate criticism: No. GST Council is a specific constitutional body (Article 279A) for tax policy; it is not cited as an overlapping mandate with Zonal Councils in the redundancy literature.

Finance Commission (option c) — some overlap in fiscal coordination discussions: Yes, critics note some thematic overlap. NDC (option d) — overlapping mandate before dissolution: Yes. GST Council is the odd one out — it does not appear in the standard redundancy criticism of Zonal Councils.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) Finance Commission is the competing distractor — students may hesitate because Finance Commission and Zonal Councils both discuss Centre-State fiscal matters. However, the Finance Commission has a constitutionally mandated, time-bound, and specific remit (revenue distribution) — it does not perform the same broad inter-state coordination function. The GST Council is the true odd one out because it is a specialised tax body, not a general federal coordination forum, and is not cited in critiques of Zonal Council redundancy.
solution.final_explanation:
The institutional redundancy critique of Zonal Councils involves identifying which bodies perform similar coordination functions.

• Option (a) — Inter-State Council: The ISC's mandate to discuss inter-state disputes and coordination directly overlaps with Zonal Councils' agenda — a commonly cited redundancy, especially since ISC covers all states and Zonal Councils cover zones.
• Option (b) — GST Council: The odd one out. GST Council (Article 279A) is a specialised constitutional body focused exclusively on GST rate-setting, exemption management, and revenue apportionment. It is not a general federal coordination forum and does not appear in scholarly or commission critiques of Zonal Council redundancy.
• Option (c) — Finance Commission: Critics note that fiscal federalism discussions in Zonal Councils can overlap with Finance Commission's territory on resource allocation — though the Commission's formal mandate is distinct.
• Option (d) — NDC: Before its effective dissolution post-2014, NDC (national planning coordination body) overlapped with Zonal Councils' economic and social planning discussions — a cited redundancy.

Value Addition:
• GST Council was inserted as Article 279A by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 — making it a constitutional body unlike Zonal Councils.
• The Punchhi Commission criticised the proliferation of overlapping federal bodies and called for clearer mandates.
• NITI Aayog's Governing Council is now seen as partly filling NDC's role — adding a new layer to the redundancy discussion.

solution.concept_anchor: Punchhi Commission — Zonal Councils as primary dispute forum before courts

statement_analysis.statement: The Sarkaria Commission recommended that Zonal Councils should meet at least twice a year to be effective instruments of Centre-State coordination.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State Relations (1988 report) specifically recommended a minimum meeting frequency of twice a year for Zonal Councils.

statement_analysis.statement: The Punchhi Commission recommended that Zonal Councils should be empowered as the primary forum for resolving inter-state disputes before parties approach the courts or Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: The Punchhi Commission (2010 report) viewed Zonal Councils as underutilised and recommended they be the first port of call for inter-state disputes, functioning as a dispute-prevention mechanism before judicial escalation.

statement_analysis.statement: Both the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions recommended that the chairmanship of Zonal Councils be transferred from the Union Home Minister to the Prime Minister to elevate their political importance.
statement_analysis.reason: Neither commission recommended changing the chairmanship from the Home Minister to the PM. Both accepted the existing structure while recommending better utilisation — not structural chairmanship changes.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is the strong distractor because both Commissions did recommend structural improvements, and a student may assume chairmanship elevation was one of them.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Sarkaria Commission's 'twice a year' meeting frequency recommendation is a documented fact.
Statement 2 is correct — Punchhi Commission's recommendation on Zonal Councils as primary dispute forums is documented.
Statement 3 is incorrect — neither commission proposed changing the chairmanship from the Home Minister to the PM. This is a plausible-sounding but fabricated recommendation.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Statement 3 is not — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is constructed as a scope-extension trap: both commissions did make structural recommendations for Zonal Councils, so adding one more (chairmanship change) sounds plausible. Students who know the commissions recommended 'strengthening' Zonal Councils may not remember whether chairmanship was specifically discussed. The key is that both commissions viewed the existing structure (including Home Minister's chairmanship) as adequate — the problem was underutilisation, not structural design.
solution.final_explanation:
Commission recommendations on Zonal Councils reveal the persistent gap between institutional design and operational reality.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Sarkaria Commission (report 1988) explicitly recommended meetings 'at least twice a year' — recognising that infrequent meetings were undermining the utility of Zonal Councils as coordination forums. This recommendation was not enacted as a statutory obligation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Punchhi Commission (report 2010) went further by recommending that Zonal Councils should function as the mandatory first step before inter-state disputes reach Parliament or the Supreme Court. This would make Zonal Councils a structured pre-litigation forum.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Neither commission recommended transferring chairmanship from the Home Minister to the Prime Minister. Both accepted the existing structural design. The PM's chairmanship of the ISC is a separate and already existing arrangement — there was no commission recommendation to merge or replicate this for Zonal Councils.

Value Addition:
• Both commissions characterised Zonal Councils as 'underutilised instruments' — a phrase that often appears in UPSC model answers.
• Sarkaria Commission also recommended reviving the ISC — both recommendations reflected the same concern about inoperative federal forums.
• Punchhi Commission's recommendation, if implemented, would create a mandatory cooling-off period before states litigate — a significant federal design change.

solution.concept_anchor: Standing Committees — real work of Zonal Councils; full meetings are infrequent
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct, and students may assume that because R explains the operational reality it must also causally explain A — missing that R is an effect, not a cause.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes — Standing Committees of senior civil servants (Chief Secretaries) do the preparatory groundwork, and the Ministry of Home Affairs provides secretariat support to all five Zonal Councils.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? Yes — full Zonal Council meetings are infrequent due to absence of mandatory frequency requirements, with meetings depending on political will.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? No — the infrequency of full meetings explains WHY Standing Committees are important, but it does not explain why the MHA provides secretariat support. The MHA's role flows from the Home Minister's chairmanship and the 1956 Act's design — not from meeting infrequency.
Both A and R are correct, but R does NOT explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The Standing Committee structure and the MHA's secretariat role are two distinct institutional features of Zonal Councils — both factual but causally independent.

Assertion (A): Factually correct. The Ministry of Home Affairs provides secretariat support to all five Zonal Councils from New Delhi. Each Zonal Council has a Standing Committee composed of Chief Secretaries of constituent states that prepares the ground before full council meetings convene.

Reason (R): Factually correct. There is no mandatory meeting frequency prescribed under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. Historical record shows several councils went years without full meetings. This infrequency has been a long-standing criticism, prompting the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation for twice-yearly meetings.

Causal relationship: R does not explain A. The MHA's secretariat role is a structural choice rooted in the Home Minister's permanent chairmanship — not a response to infrequent full meetings. Infrequency of full meetings explains the relative importance of Standing Committees operationally but does not explain who provides secretariat support.

Value Addition:
• Standing Committees meet far more regularly than full Zonal Councils — they are the operational nerve centre.
• MHA providing secretariat support to all five councils ensures uniform institutional memory and agenda-setting.
• The Zonal Council secretariat maintains records of all recommendations, decisions, and action-taken reports from previous meetings.

Pair 4 — Goa/Western: Correct. Goa's geographic and economic linkage to Maharashtra places it in the Western Zone. Three pairs are correct — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Chhattisgarh's zone assignment is the geographic swap trap. Students may associate Chhattisgarh with western or central India loosely but incorrectly assign it to the Western Zone, which is strictly the coastal western states (Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra). Chhattisgarh was carved from Madhya Pradesh in 2000 and inherited its parent state's Central Zone placement — a post-1956 addition that requires updated zone knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
Zone-wise state mapping requires systematic memorisation — geographic intuition alone produces errors.

• Rajasthan/Northern — Correct: Rajasthan's northern and northwestern position, alongside Punjab and Haryana, places it in the Northern Zonal Council.
• Chhattisgarh/Western — Incorrect: Chhattisgarh is in the Central Zonal Council. Created in 2000 by bifurcating Madhya Pradesh, it was assigned to the Central Zone. The Western Zone covers Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, and the UT of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu.
• Odisha/Eastern — Correct: Odisha is firmly in the Eastern Zonal Council. Its borders with West Bengal and Jharkhand (both Eastern Zone) confirm the placement.
• Goa/Western — Correct: Goa was a late entrant to the formal state system (1987) but was administratively linked to the Western Zone alongside Maharashtra since before statehood.

Three pairs are correct — option (c).

Value Addition:
• Jharkhand, like Chhattisgarh, was carved from an existing state (Bihar) in 2000 — but Jharkhand moved to the Eastern Zone (with its parent Bihar), while Chhattisgarh stayed Central.
• Karnataka borders both the Southern and Western Zone states — but Karnataka is in the Southern Zonal Council.
• Remembering 'no UT in Central Zone' helps anchor the Central Zone states: UP, Uttarakhand, MP, Chhattisgarh.

solution.concept_anchor: Sikkim added to NEC in 2002, not 1975
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly identifies 1971 as the year of the NEC Act but incorrectly states the NEC originally covered 8 states — it originally covered 7; Sikkim was added later.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Zonal Councils were NOT created by a constitutional amendment — they were created by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, a statutory instrument.
Evaluate (b): NEC Act, 1971 is correct, but '8 states from its inception' is incorrect — original NEC had 7 states; Sikkim was added in 2002.
Confirm (c): Sikkim's addition to the NEC occurred in 2002 through a legislative amendment — correct pairing of Sikkim with 2002.
Eliminate (d): NEC's mandate is not identical to the five Zonal Councils — NEC has broader regional planning and development functions.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Sikkim/NEC temporal trap is precisely constructed: Sikkim became India's 22nd state in 1975, a commonly known fact. Students who conflate the year of Sikkim's accession to India (1975) with its inclusion in the NEC (2002) will dismiss option (c) as incorrect. The 27-year gap between statehood and NEC membership is the specific precision being tested.
solution.final_explanation:
NEC composition and timeline requires separating the year of Sikkim's statehood from its NEC membership.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Zonal Councils were not created by a constitutional amendment. They were established under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 — ordinary parliamentary legislation. No article of the Constitution establishes them.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The NEC was indeed created in 1971, but it originally covered 7 states (the 'Seven Sisters': Arunachal, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura). Sikkim was added as the 8th member in 2002 — not from inception.
• Option (c) — Correct: Sikkim was added to the North-Eastern Council in 2002 through an amendment to the NEC Act — a full 27 years after Sikkim became India's 22nd state in 1975. This is the correctly matched pair.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: NEC has a broader mandate than the five Zonal Councils — it includes regional economic planning and development, not just advisory coordination on public order and inter-state infrastructure.

Value Addition:
• The 'Seven Sisters' metaphor for NE states predates Sikkim's inclusion — after 2002, the region informally became 'Eight Sisters'.
• NEC secretariat is in Shillong — the only regional coordination body headquartered outside Delhi.
• NEC's development mandate reflects the strategic and infrastructural needs of India's northeast frontier.

solution.concept_anchor: PM chairs ISC; Home Minister chairs Zonal Councils — not interchangeable
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students associate the Prime Minister with all major Centre-State coordination bodies and may not recall that the PM's chairmanship is specifically for the ISC, not Zonal Councils.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): Prime Minister chairs the Inter-State Council under Article 263 — not the Zonal Councils.
Eliminate (c): Deputy Prime Minister has no designated role as chair of Zonal Councils — this is a plausible-fabrication.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is the most direct test of the PM-vs-HM chairmanship confusion — the single most common error students make on Zonal Council questions. The PM's visibility in cooperative federalism (NITI Aayog, ISC) creates a strong cognitive association between the PM and inter-state coordination. Students who have not specifically memorised that it is the Home Minister — not the PM — who chairs Zonal Councils will default to option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The identity of the Zonal Council Chairman is a high-frequency, high-error UPSC question.

• Option (a) — Correct: The Union Home Minister is the permanent Chairman of all five Zonal Councils under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. This is a single chairperson for all five zones — not different ministers for different zones. The Home Minister's role reflects the law, order, and internal security dimension of these coordination forums.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Prime Minister chairs the Inter-State Council established under Article 263 — a national-level constitutional body. PM does not chair Zonal Councils.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: There is no provision for a Deputy Prime Minister to chair Zonal Councils — the designation 'Deputy PM' itself is not a constitutional office.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Finance Minister heads the GST Council (as Chairperson) and is associated with Finance Commission deliberations — not Zonal Councils.

Value Addition:
• The single chairperson for all five zones ensures uniform Centre-State interface and prevents fragmented regional power centres.
• Vice-Chairmanship rotates annually among the Chief Ministers of constituent states.
• Political significance: Home Minister's permanent chairmanship reinforces Centre's coordinating authority — a critique raised by some federalism scholars.
